summary: This version of the library builds a Map<String, Book> so a whole Book object can be found from its title, instead of just the author's name. Because the book list is left empty here, the lookup demonstrates the "not found" branch.

lines.text: Map is the interface for collections that pair each key with one value; you program against this type so the concrete implementation can change later.
HashMap is the standard Map implementation, storing entries in no particular order but finding them very quickly.
The list of Book objects is the primary collection; the map built below is a secondary index into it.
The key is the title and the value is the entire Book, so one lookup gives access to the author, the genre, and anything else the object holds.
Walking the list once fills the map, keeping the two collections in agreement.
put stores the pairing; calling it again with the same title would replace the earlier entry, since map keys are unique.
Naming the search term in a variable means it appears once and can be reused in the messages below.
get returns the matching Book, or null when the map holds no entry for that key — it does not throw an error.
Always check a map lookup for null before using the result, otherwise a missing key becomes a NullPointerException.
Concatenating the object into a string calls its toString method, which is why Book should override it.
Holding the whole object rather than a single field is what makes several details reachable from one lookup.

lines.code: System.out.println("No book found for title: " + titleToLookUp);
lines.text: With the list still empty the map has no entries, so this is the branch that actually runs.
